title: Keyhole surgery

confidence.note: The key operations are dated in surgeons' records and in histories built on interviews and letters. Priority was long credited to Philippe Mouret in 1987; historians now agree Erich Mühe removed a gallbladder by laparoscope in 1985, though some accounts still call Mouret's operation the first.

people: Kurt Semm (1927–2003), German gynecologist and laparoscopy pioneer
Erich Mühe (born 1938), chief surgeon at the Böblingen county hospital
Jacques Perissat, French surgeon who popularized the operation
summary: A German surgeon removed a gallbladder through a telescope in 1985 and was laughed at. Within a decade keyhole surgery had remade the operating room.
body: On 12 September 1980 the German gynecologist Kurt Semm took out an appendix through a laparoscope, a telescope passed into the gas-filled abdomen. Five years later almost to the day, Erich Mühe, chief surgeon at the county hospital in Böblingen, used Semm's methods and an instrument of his own, the "Galloscope," to remove a gallbladder. By March 1987 he had done 97. Colleagues mocked it as "Mickey Mouse surgery": surgical thinking held that big problems required big incisions.

Credit went to France instead. On 17 March 1987 Philippe Mouret of Lyon removed a gallbladder by laparoscope during a gynecological operation, and colleagues including François Dubois and Jacques Perissat refined and promoted the method. In April 1989 Perissat's videotape, shown in a side booth at an American surgical meeting, drew a bigger crowd than the main lectures. Within a few years the keyhole operation had displaced open surgery as the standard treatment for gallstones.
Robots followed: in 2000 the da Vinci system won FDA approval for general laparoscopic procedures.

myth.tradition: Philippe Mouret performed the first laparoscopic gallbladder removal, in Lyon in 1987.
myth.record: Erich Mühe did it in Böblingen on 12 September 1985 and had done dozens more before Mouret's first. German surgeons ignored him, and his work was only officially honored in 1992.

title: The cochlear implant

confidence.note: The first implantations and the FDA approval are documented by the pioneers and regulators. Sources differ on emphasis: the first FDA approval in 1984 was for House's single-channel device, and the first multichannel approval followed in 1985.

people: John Doyle, neurosurgeon who worked with House
Graeme Clark, Australian developer of a multichannel implant
Ingeborg Hochmair and Erwin Hochmair, Austrian developers of a multichannel implant
summary: A wire in the inner ear gave deaf people a sense of sound. It also opened one of medicine's sharpest disputes over what counts as a disability.
body: On 9 January 1961 the Los Angeles otologist William House and the neurosurgeon John Doyle implanted a single electrode in the inner ear of a deaf patient, following a 1957 attempt by André Djourno and Charles Eyriès in Paris. House's single-channel device, made with 3M, became the first cochlear implant approved by the FDA, in 1984. Multichannel implants, which send different sounds to different parts of the cochlea, won out: Ingeborg and Erwin Hochmair's was first implanted in December 1977, Graeme Clark's in August 1978. Many Deaf people opposed implanting children as a threat to sign language and Deaf identity.

title: Deep brain stimulation

confidence.note: Benabid and Pollak's 1987 paper and the FDA approval records fix the dates. One review dates the Parkinson's approval to 2001, but the FDA's own record gives 14 January 2002.

people: Mahlon R. DeLong, Emory University neurologist
summary: A surgeon testing a target in a patient's brain found that rapid electrical pulses stopped the tremor. He replaced the knife with an adjustable implant.
body: In 1987 the Grenoble neurosurgeon Alim-Louis Benabid was about to make a small lesion in the thalamus of a patient with essential tremor. Testing the spot with an electrical probe, he found that just below 100 pulses a second the tremor stopped, and returned when the current went off. With the neurologist Pierre Pollak he made the test a treatment: an implanted, adjustable and reversible stimulator instead of a permanent lesion. Drawing on Mahlon DeLong's monkey studies, they turned to the subthalamic nucleus for Parkinson's disease from 1993. The FDA approved stimulation for tremor in July 1997 and for advanced Parkinson's in January 2002.

title: From AZT to combination therapy

confidence.note: Approval dates, conference reports and US mortality statistics are all documented by the FDA, CDC and NIH. The broad story, from a modestly useful single drug to combination therapy and prevention, is not in dispute.

summary: The first AIDS drug bought patients months. A decade later, three drugs at once turned a death sentence into a manageable infection.
body: On 19 March 1987 the FDA approved the first drug for AIDS: AZT, or zidovudine, a compound first developed as a possible cancer treatment. The same day, under pressure from activists, the agency issued rules opening promising unapproved drugs to desperate patients. AZT lowered the amount of virus in the blood but gave only a modest gain in life expectancy.

The turn came almost a decade later. The first protease inhibitor was approved in 1995, and in 1996 three-drug combinations, called highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), were the news of the international AIDS conference in Vancouver. In 1997 AIDS deaths in the United States fell by 47 percent.

Treatment then became prevention, and went global. PEPFAR, announced by President George W. Bush in 2003, committed $15 billion over five years, mainly to the hardest-hit countries. In 2012 the FDA approved a daily pill, Truvada, to prevent infection (PrEP); in 2014 the PARTNER study found no sexual transmission from partners whose treatment kept the virus undetectable, the basis of the message "Undetectable = Untransmittable"; and in June 2025 the FDA approved lenacapavir, an injection given twice a year, for PrEP.

links.note: The epidemic these drugs were made to fight.

title: Statins

confidence.note: Endo's own account and the published papers date the discovery, and the FDA approval and the 4S trial are matters of record. Some details, such as the dog lymphomas that halted compactin, rest on company reports Endo himself describes as rumor.

place: Tokyo, Japan, and the United States
people: Akira Endo, biochemist at Sankyo who discovered compactin
Akira Yamamoto, Osaka physician who first gave compactin to patients
Alfred Alberts, Merck scientist who found lovastatin
summary: A Japanese chemist searching molds for a cholesterol blocker found one in 1973. It took two decades, and a scare over dogs, to prove statins saved lives.
body: Akira Endo, a biochemist at the Japanese drug company Sankyo, went looking for a cholesterol-lowering drug the way Alexander Fleming had found penicillin: in molds. From 1971 his team screened broths from thousands of fungi; after 3,800 strains one showed strong activity, and in July 1973 they isolated compactin from *Penicillium citrinum*. It blocks HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that controls the body's own production of cholesterol. Endo described it in 1976: the first statin.

The road to patients was rocky. Compactin did not work in rats, though it did in hens, dogs and monkeys. In 1978 the physician Akira Yamamoto gave it to patients with inherited high cholesterol, whose levels fell by roughly 30 percent. In 1980 Sankyo dropped it amid reports of lymphoma in dogs given enormous doses, and Merck paused its own close relative, lovastatin. Merck resumed, and lovastatin (Mevacor) became the first statin approved, in 1987.

The decisive evidence that this saved lives came in 1994, when the Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study linked a 35 percent fall in LDL cholesterol to a 40 percent drop in deaths from coronary heart disease.

links.note: Fleming's mold inspired Endo's search of fungi.

title: Prozac and the SSRI era

confidence.note: The FDA's approval record fixes the date, and the drug's development is documented in published papers. The low-serotonin theory of depression is contested; a 2022 umbrella review found no consistent support for it, though it did not test whether the drugs work.

people: David T. Wong, Eli Lilly biochemist on the team that found fluoxetine
Bryan Molloy, Eli Lilly chemist on the team
summary: Prozac made antidepressants a household word and spread the idea of a serotonin 'chemical imbalance.' The drug was real; the theory was weaker.
body: Fluoxetine was picked out at Eli Lilly in 1972 as the most potent and selective of 55 related compounds that block the reuptake of serotonin. After trials from 1984 to 1987, the FDA approved it as Prozac on 29 December 1987. It was not the first such drug sold: zimelidine was marketed in 1982 and withdrawn over side effects. SSRIs helped popularize the idea that depression is a "chemical imbalance" of serotonin, but a 2022 umbrella review found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by low serotonin.

myth.tradition: Depression is caused by too little serotonin, and Prozac works by correcting the deficit.
myth.record: The low-serotonin idea was widely publicized from the 1990s with the SSRIs, but reviews of the main lines of research find no consistent support for it. Whether the drugs relieve symptoms is a separate question.

title: The campaign to end polio

confidence.note: The 1988 resolution, the certification of type 2 and type 3 eradication, and case counts come from WHO and CDC surveillance. The 1988 baseline of 350,000 cases is an estimate.

summary: In 1988 polio paralyzed an estimated 350,000 people a year. Cases have fallen by over 99 percent, but the last stretch has proved the hardest.
body: In 1988 the World Health Assembly resolved to eradicate polio, launching the Global Polio Eradication Initiative; Rotary International had pressed for the effort from the start. Wild polio then caused an estimated 350,000 cases in more than 125 countries, and cases have since fallen by more than 99 percent. Wild type 2 was certified eradicated in 2015 and type 3 in 2019, but type 1 still circulates in Afghanistan and Pakistan. The oral vaccine complicates the endgame: where immunity is very low, its weakened virus can circulate, mutate and regain the power to paralyze, causing 672 cases between January 2023 and June 2024.

links.note: The Salk and Sabin vaccines made eradication thinkable.
The only human disease eradicated so far, and the model.

title: The Human Genome Project

confidence.note: The project's milestones are documented by the agencies that ran it and in published papers. What is often misremembered is what "complete" meant: the 2003 sequence covered over 90 percent of the genome, and the last gaps were closed only in 2022.

place: United States, Britain and partner countries
people: Francis Collins, director of the US National Human Genome Research Institute
J. Craig Venter, head of the rival company Celera
summary: A 13-year, multinational effort read the human DNA sequence, raced a private company, and declared victory in 2003. The last 8 percent took until 2022.
body: In 1990 an international consortium set out to read the whole of human DNA, about 3 billion chemical letters, in order. In the United States the Human Genome Project was funded by the Department of Energy and the National Institutes of Health; the Wellcome Trust helped lead it from Britain. It was budgeted at $3 billion over 15 years and drew in thousands of researchers.

Midway, it became a race. Craig Venter's company Celera set out to sequence the genome privately, commercialize the data and seek patents on genes. The public consortium released its data rapidly, a policy President Clinton and Prime Minister Blair applauded in a joint statement in 2000. In June 2000 a draft covering 90 percent of the genome was celebrated at the White House, and the consortium's paper describing it appeared in 2001. Celera's sequence was eventually deposited in the public database GenBank as well.

In April 2003, two years ahead of schedule, the consortium declared the sequence essentially complete. It was a reference genome assembled from more than one person, and it supported an estimate that humans have between 20,000 and 25,000 protein-coding genes.

"Essentially complete" meant over 90 percent, as close as the technology of the time allowed. The remaining 8 percent, long repetitive stretches around the centromeres and the short arms of five chromosomes, stayed missing or wrong for nearly two decades. On 31 March 2022 the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium, using long-read sequencing, announced the first truly complete sequence, adding nearly 200 million letters and 99 predicted protein-coding genes. Even that left out the Y chromosome.
Meanwhile the price collapsed. The draft alone cost about $300 million; by late 2015 a high-quality human genome could be sequenced for under $1,500.

myth.tradition: The Human Genome Project read one person's complete genome and finished in 2003.
myth.record: Its reference sequence came from more than one person, and in 2003 it covered over 90 percent of the genome. The last 8 percent, mostly repetitive DNA, was filled in only in 2022, and the Y chromosome later still.

links.note: The structure that made the sequence meaningful.
